relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: Solomon completes everything his royal desire set before him.
The Divine appears again after the architecture is finished.
The prayer is heard, and the house receives the name, eyes, and heart of presence.
Yet the promise immediately turns from building to integrity and justice.
Dynastic continuity remains conditional rather than automatic.
Children and rulers can turn away even after sacred dedication.
Temple and land are not shields against the consequences of betrayal.
A monument of glory can become a ruin that asks uncomfortable questions.
The narrative interprets collapse through abandoned covenant, though suffering must never be simplistically assigned to victims.
Twenty years of temple and palace construction close.
Solomon pays his ally with twenty Galilean cities, moving communities through royal agreement.
Hiram inspects the gift and finds it inadequate.
The disappointed name Cabul preserves tension beneath diplomatic brotherhood.
Gold still flows from Hiram toward Solomon.
The monuments and fortified cities are built through a levy of human labor.
Gezer enters Solomon's realm through fire, massacre, and a marriage gift.
The conquered city becomes a royal construction site.
Other cities extend storage and control into wilderness.
Solomon's desire fills the land with warehouses, chariots, horsemen, and buildings.
The narrative identifies surviving peoples outside Israel.
Those not destroyed are made hereditary forced laborers, revealing survival without liberation.
Israelites are assigned military and administrative roles instead of slave labor.
Hundreds of officers rule those doing the work.
Pharaoh's daughter moves to the house built for her while the city infrastructure expands.
Regular sacrifice integrates the new temple into royal time.
A fleet is built on Edomite shore.
Tyrian seafarers bring knowledge the royal project cannot generate alone.
Ophir's distant gold arrives at Solomon's throne, while its human and ecological source remains unseen.

contemplative_note: The chapter breaks the illusion that sacred success is harmless. Behind temple, palace, fortification, and fleet stand transferred cities, conquered residents, ethnic forced labor, military systems, and extracted gold. Integrity is the true house the Divine asks Solomon to build.
